about.title: Payday Loan Calculator - Short-Term Cost, APR & Rollover Impact Estimator
about.description: The Payday Loan Calculator estimates total repayment, finance charges, and effective APR for short-term payday loans. Model rollover scenarios, compare alternatives, and understand how fees compound over time to avoid debt traps and plan responsible borrowing.

howTo.title: How to Use the Payday Loan Calculator

steps.title: Enter Loan Amount
steps.description: Input the cash advance amount you plan to borrow.

steps.title: Add Fees & Term
steps.description: Include flat fees or percentage-based charges and select the typical 14–30 day term.

steps.title: Model Rollovers
steps.description: Add the number of renewals/rollovers if you cannot repay on time.

steps.title: Review Total Cost & APR
steps.description: See total repayment, effective APR, and how charges escalate with rollovers.

steps.title: Compare Alternatives
steps.description: Test options like installment loans or paycheck advances to reduce cost.

tips: Avoid rollovers—fees can snowball and drastically raise effective APR.
Consider credit union small-dollar loans or employer advances as cheaper alternatives.
Repay early if allowed to minimize fees and interest.

features.title: Effective APR Estimation
features.description: Converts fees and short terms into an annualized APR for apples-to-apples comparisons.

features.title: Rollover Cost Modeling
features.description: Estimate how multiple renewals increase total fees and repayment amount.

features.title: Repayment Breakdown
features.description: See principal vs. fees to understand true borrowing cost.

features.title: Alternative Comparison
features.description: Compare payday loans with installment or personal loans to lower costs.

faq.a: A short-term, small-dollar loan typically due on your next payday, often with high fees and very high effective APR.

faq.q: Why is the APR so high?
faq.a: Short repayment periods combined with fixed fees produce very high annualized rates when converted to APR.
Consider credit union small-dollar loans, payment plans, employer paycheck advances, or negotiating with creditors.
